meta.title: Autonomous seeding robot vs hired labor, quarter-acre scale

nodes.text: An autonomous seeding robot plants a quarter-acre plot at lower cost per bed than hired labor within one season
A garden-bed-scale autonomous seeding robot can be bought today for about $8,000
The largest garden-scale autonomous seeder covers at most 3 by 6 meters, 18 square meters
Hired crop labor costs about $17 per hour at the US median
A walk-behind push seeder lets one worker seed a full 30-inch bed in one or two walking passes
Amortized over one season, the robot's cost per bed planted is lower than the hired-labor cost per bed
A quarter acre is far too small to amortize any autonomous seeder's capital cost within one season
Garden-scale automation costs thousands of dollars while covering only a few beds
Field-scale seeding robots cost tens of thousands of dollars and are designed for fields of 20 to 30 hectares

holes.why: No source supports the comparison, and the grounded numbers imply its opposite by roughly two orders of magnitude. The only garden-bed-scale robot on the market costs $7,995 (s1, pricing section) and covers 18 square meters, about 4 standard 30-inch beds (s1, dimensions section), so one-season amortization is roughly $2,000 per bed before installation and upkeep. Hired labor at the $17.15/hr US median (s3) costs under $20 per bed even at a deliberately generous full hour per bed, and a push seeder finishes a bed in one or two walking passes (s4), so the real figure is lower. Field-scale robots amortize worse here: $60,000 (s6) against a 20-to-30-hectare design target (s5) is 80 to 120 times the plot in question.
